place: A cleared garden plot behind a homestead, tilled soil, edge of a small orchard nearby.
outcome: The gardener pushes the whole apple into loose soil instead of saving out its seeds. The flesh has no use buried whole: it goes soft and rots within days, feeding worms and souring the soil right there. But a few of the pips inside are viable, and if the rotting flesh doesn't smother them first, two or three seedlings may push up together weeks later, crowded into one hole, once the ground warms in spring. A gardener who cut the fruit for seed and spaced the pips would have done far better.

stress: planting the whole fruit instead of extracted seed
temptation: a rule that says planting an apple always grows an apple tree, naming the fruit by name

place: A row of bean seedlings in a kitchen garden, recently sprouted, clay-heavy soil that drains slowly.
lines: give them more, they look dry
outcome: The gardener waters the seedlings three times in one day because the topsoil looks pale, not realizing the clay beneath is still soaked from yesterday. The extra water has nowhere to drain, and within days the roots sit in standing water and start to rot instead of drawing air. The leaves yellow and the stems soften at the base; by week's end most of the row is dead, and no amount of water brings it back. Overwatering kills as surely as drought, just slower and less obviously.

soil: still waterlogged, needs days to dry before replanting
stress: too much of the very thing a plant needs kills it just as dead as drought does
temptation: a hardcoded rule that more water is always good for beans

place: A root cellar shelf with a cloth sack of carrot seed saved two autumns ago, and a garden bed ready for spring sowing.
outcome: The gardener sows a handful of carrot seed that has sat in a dry sack for two winters. Seed loses vigor with age, and carrot seed keeps poorly even fresh, so only a fraction of what's sown is still alive enough to sprout. The row comes up patchy: gaps where nothing took, a scatter of seedlings where enough viable seed happened to land close together. It isn't a total loss, but it isn't the full stand a fresh packet would have given, and there was no way to tell which seeds were still good until the ground showed it.

temptation: treating all seed of a kind as identically viable regardless of age

place: A vegetable plot the household hasn't visited in weeks, bordered by open field thick with wild grasses and bindweed.
outcome: With nobody pulling weeds, wind-blown seed and creeping bindweed from the field edge take hold between the cabbage rows. Over a few weeks the weeds grow faster than the cabbages, shading their leaves and pulling water out from under them. By the time anyone looks again, half the cabbages are stunted and a few are smothered outright under bindweed. Nothing dramatic happened on any single day; it is the sum of weeks of neglect.

temptation: a rule naming cabbage and bindweed specifically instead of general growth-rate competition for light and water

place: A garden bed in early winter, ground cold but not yet frozen solid.
outcome: The gardener sows turnip seed into cold ground well past the growing season. The seed doesn't rot outright in cold dry soil, but it also doesn't have the warmth to germinate; it simply sits dormant through winter. Nothing visible happens for months. Only once the ground warms again in spring does the buried seed finally sprout, weeks later than a spring sowing would have and with no guarantee all of it survived the cold undisturbed.

place: An old apple tree past its best fruiting years, orchard corner, beside a young rootstock sapling planted last spring.
lines: cut a branch from the old tree
bind it onto the new sapling
outcome: The gardener cuts a healthy shoot from the old tree, fits it into a cut made in the young rootstock, and binds and seals the join so it doesn't dry out. If the two knit together over the following weeks, the sapling grows on as the old tree's variety, carried on stronger young roots. It takes years, not weeks, before it's old enough to fruit, and there's a real chance the graft simply fails to take if the join dries out or doesn't match up, in which case the rootstock either dies back or grows on as itself with none of the wanted fruit.

temptation: a rule that grafting always works when you graft the branch, without conditions on the cut and the seal

place: A compost heap of kitchen scraps and garden waste behind the house, turned occasionally, sitting through summer.
outcome: Nobody planted anything in the compost heap; squash seed thrown out with last month's rinds survives the pile's heat and, given the heap's rich rot and steady moisture, sprouts on its own. Within weeks a vine is climbing over the heap's edge, and by late summer it's carrying a squash nobody planned for. It's a real vegetable, free for the taking, but it's also sprawled over the compost path and its roots are pulling nutrients that would otherwise have gone into finished compost.

place: A fenced kitchen garden of leafy greens, next to a paddock where a goat is kept, fence in need of repair.
outcome: The goat finds the weak section of fence it has been leaning on for days and finally pushes through overnight. By morning it has eaten most of the greens down to bare stubble and trampled the rest flat getting around the bed. Nothing left standing is worth harvesting, and greens grow back slowly from stubble if at all; the household won't have a crop from this bed for weeks, if it recovers before frost.

place: A wheat field near ripe, golden but with some green still in the heads, weather turning uncertain.
outcome: The farmer cuts the field a little early, worried about a coming storm. Some heads are fully ripe and thresh out well, but a good portion are still green inside the husk and yield shrunken, poor grain that won't store or mill as well. Waiting the extra week would have ripened it fully, but it would also have risked losing grain to shattering heads and birds if the storm had come first; there was no clean answer, only a trade of one loss against another.

place: A young oak sapling planted a stride from the base of an old hedge, edge of an orchard.
outcome: The sapling was planted close to the hedge for a windbreak, but nobody accounted for how tall the hedge would get. Season by season the hedge grows and leans out, taking more of the sapling's light each year. By the third or fourth year the oak is thin, leaning away from the hedge toward what light it can reach, its growth well behind an unshaded tree of the same age. It isn't dead, but it may never be more than a stunted, lopsided tree unless the hedge is cut back, and by now moving the sapling risks killing it outright.

outcome: The player glances around at their feet for a moment, expecting an easy pick-up. Loose stones aren't common in open grassland; turf covers most of the ground, so a quick look has real odds of coming up empty. This time nothing is in easy reach, and the player either goes home without a stone or has to commit to a longer, more deliberate search than a glance.

place: A worked stone quarry face, loose rubble at the base, chisel and hammer left by a previous mason.
outcome: Stone is the whole point of a quarry, so finding one at all is nearly certain; the real work is picking a piece worth taking and freeing it. The player spots a promising seam, works the chisel into it, and knocks a usable block loose. It takes real effort and a few minutes, and a slip with the hammer could just as easily crack the piece wrong and waste it, but there was never any doubt stone was here to find.

place: Damp forest floor after recent rain, leaf litter thick, a known patch where mushrooms sometimes come up.

outcome: A quick glance across the leaf litter would likely miss the mushrooms entirely; they sit low, mottled, and easy to pass over. The player commits to a slow, careful search, turning over leaves and checking damp hollows, and the extra time pays off: several mushrooms turn up that a glance would have walked past. It costs the better part of an hour rather than a few seconds, and there's still no guarantee of finding enough for a meal if the patch is thin this week.

It isn't what was sought and doesn't answer any question by itself, but it's there now, sitting in the turned dirt, and someone has to decide whether it matters.

Only if the player waits, and the river rises overnight and reshuffles the gravel, would coming back tomorrow actually mean something different. Right now, twice in a row is just once, done slowly.

place: A steep dirt bank above a farm track, ordinary earth, no stone visible on the surface before a night of heavy rain.
outcome: A night of hard rain washes a layer of loose soil off the steep bank, exposing a scatter of stones that had been sitting under the surface all along, unseen. Nobody did anything; the world simply changed what was on top. A player passing the next day and glancing at the bank now finds stones easily, where a glance the week before would have found bare earth and nothing else. The place didn't change what it held, only what was showing.
